items.followUp: Explain the lock-and-key model of enzyme action.

rubric.why: Identifies how the substrate binds to the enzyme.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the substrate binds to, or fits, the enzyme’s active site.

rubric.why: Describes the induced adjustment and resulting complex.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that substrate binding changes the active site’s shape to fit the substrate, forming an enzyme–substrate complex.

modelAnswer: The substrate binds to the enzyme’s active site.
This binding causes the active site to change shape and fit the substrate, forming an enzyme–substrate complex.

items.followUp: Name four dietary sources of carbohydrates.

rubric.why: Gives examples of protein-rich foods from animal sources.
rubric.how: Award for naming two suitable animal sources of protein.

rubric.why: Gives examples of protein-rich foods from plant sources.
rubric.how: Award for naming two suitable plant sources of protein.

modelAnswer: Animal sources of proteins include meat, fish, eggs and milk.
Plant sources include pulses, beans, peas and nuts.

items.followUp: Define transpiration and state one factor that affects its rate.

rubric.why: Shows that transpiration from leaves creates the pull.
rubric.how: Award for linking the pull to water loss or evaporation from the leaves.

rubric.why: Identifies the upward movement of water through the plant.
rubric.how: Award for describing the force that draws water upward through xylem, from roots toward leaves.

modelAnswer: Transpirational pull is the force produced by water loss from leaves during transpiration.
It draws water upward from the roots through the xylem.

items.followUp: What is blood clotting, and how do platelets help in it?

rubric.why: Defines platelets as formed elements of blood rather than whole cells.
rubric.how: Award for identifying platelets as small cell fragments (thrombocytes) present in blood.

rubric.why: States the principal function of platelets.
rubric.how: Award for stating that platelets help blood clot and stop bleeding at a wound.

modelAnswer: Platelets, also called thrombocytes, are small cell fragments present in the blood.
They help in blood clotting and prevent excessive bleeding from a wound.

items.followUp: Explain the branches of biology called anatomy, physiology, genetics and ecology.

rubric.why: Checks knowledge of four branches and what each studies.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each correctly named branch paired with its field of study; accept any four suitable branches.

modelAnswer: Morphology studies the external form and structure of organisms.
Anatomy studies the internal structure of organisms.
Physiology studies the functions of different parts of organisms.
Genetics studies heredity and variation in organisms.

items.followUp: Describe the structure and functions of the cell membrane.

rubric.why: Identifies the nucleus and its general role in the cell.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the nucleus as a cell organelle that controls cell activities.

rubric.why: Describes the boundary around the nucleus and its pores.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a double nuclear membrane/envelope surrounds the nucleus and has pores.

rubric.why: Includes the fluid material and/or chromatin within the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award for naming nucleoplasm and describing chromatin as present in it.

rubric.why: Recognises the genetic material in the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award for stating that chromatin forms chromosomes or contains DNA/genetic material.

rubric.why: Describes the nucleolus and its role in ribosome formation.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the nucleolus and linking it to the formation of ribosomes.

modelAnswer: The nucleus is a membrane-bound organelle that controls the activities of the cell.
It is surrounded by a double nuclear membrane (nuclear envelope) containing pores.
The nucleus contains nucleoplasm, in which chromatin is present.
Chromatin contains DNA and forms chromosomes during cell division.
The nucleolus is present in the nucleus and helps form ribosomes.

items.followUp: Compare the main characteristics of Kingdom Monera and Kingdom Protista.

rubric.why: Checks key plant characteristics.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for plants being multicellular with cellulose cell walls, and 1 mark for chlorophyll/photosynthesis (or their generally autotrophic nutrition).

rubric.why: Checks key fungal characteristics.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for fungi being heterotrophic and absorbing nutrients, and 1 mark for a suitable feature such as chitin cell walls, hyphae/mycelium, or spore reproduction.

modelAnswer: Kingdom Fungi: fungi are eukaryotic and mostly multicellular; their bodies are usually made of hyphae forming a mycelium.
Fungi lack chlorophyll and obtain food heterotrophically by absorption; their cell walls contain chitin and many reproduce by spores.
Kingdom Plantae: plants are eukaryotic and multicellular, with cellulose cell walls and chloroplasts containing chlorophyll.
Most plants make their own food by photosynthesis.

items.followUp: Describe the light reactions of photosynthesis and state where they occur.

rubric.why: Identifies the location of the dark reactions.
rubric.how: Award for stating that dark reactions occur in the stroma of chloroplasts.

rubric.why: Describes carbon dioxide fixation in the cycle.
rubric.how: Award for stating that carbon dioxide combines with RuBP (ribulose bisphosphate).

rubric.why: Checks the formation and reduction of the first stable product.
rubric.how: Award for stating that PGA is reduced to PGAL using ATP and NADPH.

rubric.why: Checks the products and regeneration stage of the cycle.
rubric.how: Award for stating that some PGAL is used to form glucose/carbohydrates and the rest regenerates RuBP.

rubric.why: Clarifies the relationship of dark reactions to light and photosynthetic products.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that light is not directly required, while ATP and NADPH from the light reactions are used.

modelAnswer: Dark reactions, or the Calvin cycle, take place in the stroma of chloroplasts and do not require light directly.
Carbon dioxide combines with RuBP (ribulose bisphosphate) to form an unstable compound that splits into PGA.
PGA is reduced to PGAL using ATP and NADPH produced during the light reactions.
Some PGAL is used to make glucose and other carbohydrates.
The remaining PGAL is used to regenerate RuBP, allowing the cycle to continue.
